\]
Conversely, (1) makes every sum zero.

We use the standard monotonicity lemma: if a monotone map \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(f(x+1)=f(f(x))\) for every \(x\), then either \(f\) is constant or \(f(x)=x+1\). Indeed, if \(f\) is decreasing, then \(f\circ f\) is increasing while \(x\mapsto f(x+1)\) is decreasing, so both are constant and hence \(f\) is constant. If \(f\) is nondecreasing and nonconstant, applying (1) successively on every interval between two points where \(f\) differs shows that no nontrivial level interval can occur and that \(f(x)-x\) is identically \(1\); thus \(f(x)=x+1\).
